headline: What the biggest voices in bonds are saying
bigPicture: The shared view among the market’s leading voices is that the era of cheap money is over. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September because inflation has been above its 2% goal for more than five years, and minutes released Oct 7 show most officials expect another hike by year end. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, a hotter reading than expected. The 10-year Treasury yield touched about 5.35% on Oct 7, its highest level since 2002, then eased to about 5.1% by Oct 16 as a stock selloff sent investors into Treasuries, and was still near 5.1% on Oct 20.

The pressure comes from supply as much as inflation. Federal debt has passed $40 trillion, the government keeps borrowing heavily, and traditional foreign buyers such as Japan and China are buying fewer Treasuries. Turmoil in France’s bond market, where 10-year yields topped 5% on Oct 22, is a reminder that the pressure is global, though for now it is sending some safe-haven money into Treasuries. Ray Dalio says the U.S. is nearing the limit of how much debt it can carry and that the bond bear market probably has a long way to go, and several of these investors say that makes buy-and-hold in long-term bonds riskier than it used to be.

They are not all bearish on bonds. BlackRock’s Rick Rieder calls today’s yields on high-quality, shorter-term bonds a historic opportunity and names investment-grade corporate bonds his top pick, though PIMCO’s Dan Ivascyn warns the 10-year yield could still reach 6% and expects the Fed to hold this month, then probably raise rates once more this year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blames September’s jump in inflation on an energy shock from the Iran conflict, says prices will come down once it is over, and does not expect France’s troubles to spill over to the U.S. Gundlach warns that long-term Treasuries may not protect investors the way they used to, Dalio is betting against bonds and holding gold instead, and Bill Gross now says not to own bonds at all, apart from one-year Treasury bills.
agree: Rates will stay higher for longer
Government debt is the core pressure on yields
Quality matters more than chasing extra yield
differ: High-quality bonds now pay enough to be worth owning
Long-term Treasuries may not be a safe haven next time

voices.name: Kevin Warsh
voices.where: FOMC statement and minutes; IMF–World Bank annual meetings, Bangkok
points: The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%–4.00% in a unanimous 12–0 vote, citing inflation that has run above target for more than five years.

Speaking in Bangkok on Oct 16, two days after a hotter-than-expected inflation report, he said the economy has broadly matched the Fed’s expectations since September, but gave no signal on whether it will raise rates again at its Oct 27–28 meeting. Minutes released Oct 7 show most officials expect another hike this year.

He said the Fed has made clear it will deliver price stability, and called the AI investment surge the most important upside force in the global economy, one that can add to inflation now but should bring large benefits over time, after a likely bumpy transition.

voices.name: Scott Bessent
points: On Oct 20 he said he does not expect France’s bond-market turmoil to spill over to the U.S., and that money is flowing out of some countries of concern and into Treasuries as a safe haven.

On Oct 18 he said September’s hotter inflation reading was an energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, not a sign of broad price pressure, noting that core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, had fallen four months in a row.

He said prices, and mortgage rates, should come down once the energy shock fades, and that the government is considering ending the conservatorship of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac within the next year or two.

voices.name: Mohamed El-Erian
points: He expects the global government-bond selloff to run further, because traditional big buyers of Treasuries, notably Japan and China, have been buying less. On Oct 1 he said upward pressure on yields remains the dominant theme.
He sees the core problem as a fiscal imbalance with no political appetite to fix it, which keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs for households and businesses.
He also cautions that investors anchored to a decade of ultra-low yields may be reacting to today’s levels with more fear than the fundamentals justify.
voices.quote: It has much more to do with a fundamental imbalance…

voices.name: Jeffrey Gundlach
voices.where: CNBC; interview with David Rosenberg, reported by MarketWatch
points: He said the Fed should have raised rates by half a point, not a quarter, given its own forecast that inflation won’t reach 2% until 2029.

He warned that the next recession could push long-term Treasury yields up rather than down, and on Oct 1 added that the dollar may fall rather than rise next time, as heavy government debt leaves only inflationary ways out.
He called the U.S. stock market a hollow tree: the index looks healthy only because a handful of giant companies are holding it up while most stocks have fallen well off their highs.
voices.quote: Long-term rates are going to go up because of the debt crisis…

voices.name: Bill Gross
points: He told investors not to own bonds, with the exception of one-year Treasury bills, which he noted were yielding 4.55%.

He argues debt has piled up too far, about $84 trillion of government, mortgage and corporate credit, with federal debt near 100% of GDP and an AI borrowing boom, which he links to higher inflation and slower growth.
He expects more swings in 10-year Treasury prices and urges caution on stocks, warning that higher yields will squeeze company profit margins.
voices.quote: Preserve and protect is my current investment motto.

voices.name: Ray Dalio
voices.where: Bloomberg TV interview; Greenwich Economic Forum; LinkedIn essay
points: In an Oct 13 essay he said the selloff in Treasuries is far from over: the U.S. must refinance about $10 trillion of maturing debt this year and borrow about $2.1 trillion more, while China and Japan have shifted from buying Treasuries to trimming them.

He describes a self-feeding loop in which more borrowing pushes yields up, which raises interest costs and adds still more debt, and says the debt burden relative to tax revenue is the highest since World War II. He expects it to last until higher rates slow the economy.
He favors gold over government bonds and says conditions favor betting against Treasuries, warns that other markets may weaken too, and has likened the AI investment boom to a bubble.
voices.quote: The bond bear market probably has a long way to go.

voices.name: Rick Rieder
voices.role: CIO of Global Fixed Income, BlackRock
voices.where: CNBC interview on his fourth-quarter outlook
points: On Oct 21 he called today’s yields on high-quality bonds historic: a diversified portfolio with under three years of duration and an average A- rating could yield over 7%, levels usually seen only in an economic or default crisis, which he says this is not.

Investment-grade corporate bonds are now his top pick, including debt from cash-rich tech giants such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, but he is cautious about lower-rated credit and data-center debt they don’t back.

He expects the Fed to raise rates in December but disagrees, saying higher rates hurt housing, credit cards and auto loans while doing little to slow tech spending, and warns that heavy AI bond issuance is starting to crowd out other borrowers.
voices.quote: So you don’t really have to worry about defaults of any significance.

voices.name: Dan Ivascyn
voices.where: Financial Times interview; Grant’s Fall Conference, speaking to Reuters
points: He said the 10-year Treasury yield could rise to 6%, a level not seen since 2000, calling it possible rather than a forecast, and blamed part of the recent jump on forced selling by investors using borrowed money.
On Oct 13 he said yields have probably not yet peaked: he expects the Fed to hold rates at its Oct 27–28 meeting and then probably raise them once more this year, with one or two more hikes in all.
He said housing is already weak and commercial real estate is where higher rates will bite next, and he expects Chair Warsh to keep an open mind on inflation while saying less about future moves.
voices.quote: We'll probably see a Fed on hold now.

actions: Keep an emergency fund that earns
Hold 3 to 6 months of essential expenses in a high-yield savings account, money-market fund or Treasury bills. At today’s rates, cash is earning around 4%.
The Fed just raised rates, and credit cards and home-equity lines reset with it. Paying them down is a guaranteed return.
Match bonds to when you need the money
Money needed in the next few years belongs in short-term bonds or a ladder of Treasuries that mature when you need them, not in long-term bond funds.
Duration tells you roughly how much a fund falls when yields rise 1 point. A fund with a 15-year duration can lose about 15%. The Bonds page shows this for any Treasury.
Most of these managers prefer Treasuries, investment-grade and mortgage bonds over high-yield debt right now. Chasing a little more income can mean taking a lot more risk.
Spread savings across stocks, bonds and cash, consider inflation-protected Treasuries (TIPS) for part of your bond money, and keep automatic investing on rather than trying to time the market.
